metin: During adolescence, the body's internal clock shifts, so that teenagers naturally feel sleepy later at night and wake up later in the morning. Yet most secondary schools begin early, forcing students to get up while their bodies still need rest. Several studies have found that when schools delayed their start times by as little as thirty minutes, students slept longer, arrived on time more often and performed better in morning classes. Some education experts now argue that school timetables should be adapted to adolescent biology.

Microplastics, tiny fragments of plastic less than five millimetres long, have been detected in tap water and bottled water around the world. They come from many sources, including synthetic clothing, car tyres and the breakdown of larger plastic items. Although scientists have not yet established whether the particles pose a significant risk to human health, their ubiquity has prompted calls for better filtration systems and stricter limits on plastic waste.

When the first bicycles appeared in the early nineteenth century, they had no pedals; riders pushed themselves along with their feet. Later models with a huge front wheel were fast but dangerous, and falls were common. It was only in the 1880s, with the introduction of the 'safety bicycle', which had two wheels of equal size and a chain drive, that cycling became popular with ordinary people. The bicycle gave many women in particular a new sense of freedom, allowing them to travel independently for the first time.

A placebo is a treatment with no active ingredient, such as a sugar pill. Remarkably, patients who receive placebos often report real improvements in symptoms like pain and fatigue. Researchers believe this happens partly because expectations can influence how the brain processes signals from the body. Intriguingly, some studies show that placebos can work even when patients are told they are taking a fake pill, although the effect is usually smaller.

Cities are often several degrees warmer than the surrounding countryside, a phenomenon known as the urban heat island effect. Dark surfaces such as asphalt and roofs absorb sunlight during the day and release heat at night, while the lack of vegetation reduces natural cooling. During heatwaves, this extra warmth can be deadly, particularly for elderly people. Fortunately, relatively simple measures, such as planting trees and painting roofs white, can make a considerable difference.

Each autumn, millions of monarch butterflies travel up to 4,000 kilometres from Canada and the United States to the forests of central Mexico. What makes this journey extraordinary is that no single butterfly completes the round trip; the insects that return north in spring are the descendants of those that left. Sadly, the population has plummeted in recent decades as a result of habitat loss and pesticide use, and conservationists warn that the migration itself could disappear.

Paper money first appeared in China during the Tang dynasty, when merchants began using paper receipts instead of carrying heavy strings of metal coins. By the eleventh century, the Song government had taken control of printing these notes, making them official currency. However, printing too much money eventually led to severe inflation, and the value of the notes collapsed. When Marco Polo described Chinese paper money in the thirteenth century, many Europeans found the idea hard to believe.

Of the roughly 7,000 languages spoken today, linguists estimate that nearly half could vanish by the end of this century. When the last speakers of a language die, a unique way of describing the world is lost, including knowledge about local plants, animals and traditions. Some communities have succeeded in reviving endangered languages through schools and recordings; Welsh and Hawaiian are often cited as examples. Such efforts, however, require long-term commitment and funding.

Vertical farms grow crops in stacked layers inside buildings, using artificial light and carefully controlled conditions. Supporters claim that they use up to 95 percent less water than conventional farms and allow fresh food to be produced close to consumers in cities. Critics, however, point out that the electricity needed for lighting is costly, and that so far vertical farms can profitably grow only a limited range of crops, such as lettuce and herbs. Whether they will transform agriculture or remain a niche remains to be seen.

Living near an active volcano may seem foolish, yet millions of people do so. One reason is that volcanic ash, once weathered, produces exceptionally fertile soil rich in minerals. In regions such as Java in Indonesia, farmers can harvest several crops a year on the slopes of volcanoes. Of course, the benefits come at a price: eruptions can destroy homes and fields within hours, and the timing of such events remains notoriously difficult to predict.

People who have just begun learning a skill often overestimate their ability. A beginner who has read a few articles about investing, for instance, may feel more confident than an experienced investor. Psychologists explain that the knowledge needed to perform well is often the same knowledge needed to recognise one's own mistakes. As people gain expertise, they typically become more aware of how much they do not know, and their confidence may temporarily decline.

As freshwater supplies come under pressure, many dry countries are turning to desalination, the process of removing salt from seawater. Modern plants, which mostly force water through fine membranes, supply a large share of drinking water in countries such as Israel and Saudi Arabia. Yet desalination consumes a great deal of energy, and the extremely salty waste it produces, known as brine, can harm marine ecosystems if it is discharged carelessly into the sea.

In some countries, citizens must actively register if they wish to become organ donors, whereas in others everyone is considered a donor unless they choose to opt out. Research shows that this simple difference in default settings can dramatically affect donation rates. Such policies are examples of 'nudges': small changes in the way choices are presented that encourage certain behaviour without restricting freedom. Critics argue, though, that governments should be careful not to manipulate citizens, even for good causes.

Deep in the Antarctic ice sheet lies a remarkable record of the Earth's past climate. As snow falls and is compressed into ice, it traps tiny bubbles of air. By drilling long cylinders of ice, known as cores, and analysing these bubbles, scientists can measure the concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere hundreds of thousands of years ago. The data reveal a close correlation between carbon dioxide levels and global temperatures over time.

Dogs were the first animals to be domesticated, long before cattle or sheep. Genetic evidence suggests that they descended from wolves that began living near human camps tens of thousands of years ago, perhaps attracted by leftover food. Over time, the less fearful and aggressive animals thrived alongside humans and gradually changed. The result is an extraordinary partnership: dogs today can read human gestures, such as pointing, better than chimpanzees, our closest relatives.

Social media promised to bring people closer together, and in some ways it has. Yet a growing number of studies link heavy use of these platforms to feelings of loneliness, particularly among young adults. One explanation is that online interactions may displace face-to-face contact, which is richer in emotional cues. Another is that constant exposure to carefully edited images of others' lives encourages unfavourable comparisons. The relationship is complex, however, and moderate use may have few negative effects.

The Vikings sailed across the North Atlantic, reaching Iceland, Greenland and even North America around the year 1000, without magnetic compasses. Historians believe they relied on the position of the sun, the behaviour of birds and whales, and their detailed knowledge of wind and waves. Some sagas also mention a mysterious 'sunstone' that could locate the sun on cloudy days; experiments suggest that certain crystals found in Scandinavia could indeed have served this purpose.

Artificial intelligence systems are increasingly being used to analyse medical images such as X-rays and scans. In several studies, algorithms trained on thousands of images detected certain cancers as accurately as experienced radiologists, and sometimes faster. Nevertheless, most experts see these systems as tools to support doctors rather than replace them. Algorithms can make unexpected errors when faced with images unlike those they were trained on, and they cannot discuss results with patients.

For years, coffee was viewed with suspicion by health experts, who worried about its effects on the heart. More recent research has painted a more favourable picture. Large studies suggest that moderate consumption, around three to four cups a day, is associated with a slightly lower risk of several diseases, including type 2 diabetes. However, pregnant women are still advised to limit their intake, and people who are sensitive to caffeine may experience anxiety or sleeplessness.

Mangrove forests grow along tropical coastlines, where their tangled roots stabilise the shore and shelter young fish. They also store large amounts of carbon, and studies have shown that coastal villages protected by mangroves suffered less damage during tsunamis and storms. Despite these benefits, vast areas of mangroves have been cleared for shrimp farms and tourist resorts, a trade-off that many scientists consider short-sighted.

In 1796, the English doctor Edward Jenner noticed that milkmaids who had caught cowpox, a mild disease, seemed to be protected from smallpox, which killed millions. He tested his idea by infecting a boy with material from a cowpox sore and later exposing him to smallpox; the boy did not become ill. Jenner's method, which he called vaccination, spread rapidly. Nearly two centuries later, in 1980, the World Health Organization declared smallpox eradicated.

The shift to remote work, accelerated by the pandemic, has produced mixed results. Many employees appreciate the absence of long commutes and the flexibility to organise their day. Some companies report that productivity has held steady or even risen. On the other hand, managers worry that remote work hinders the informal exchanges that spark new ideas, and some workers struggle to separate their professional and private lives. A hybrid model, combining office and home working, is emerging as a popular compromise.

In 1935, cane toads were introduced to Australia to control beetles that were damaging sugar cane crops. The plan failed badly. The toads showed little interest in the beetles but reproduced rapidly, spreading across millions of square kilometres. Because they are highly poisonous, native predators such as snakes and quolls that tried to eat them often died. Today, the cane toad is regarded as one of the most destructive invasive species in the country.

Mindfulness meditation, which involves paying attention to the present moment without judgement, has become enormously popular in schools and workplaces. Some studies indicate that regular practice can reduce stress and improve concentration. Researchers caution, however, that many early studies were small and poorly designed, and that the benefits may have been overstated. Mindfulness is not a cure for serious mental illness, they stress, although it may be a useful addition to other treatments.

Engineers have begun using giant 3D printers to construct houses by laying down layer after layer of a special concrete mixture. A small home can be printed in a matter of days, with far less waste and fewer workers than traditional methods require. Advocates believe the technology could help address housing shortages and provide shelter quickly after natural disasters. Building regulations, however, have not yet caught up with the technology, and the long-term durability of printed houses is still being studied.

Fast fashion companies produce inexpensive clothing that imitates the latest catwalk trends and reaches shops within weeks. This model has made fashionable clothes affordable for millions, but it comes with hidden costs. The textile industry is a major source of water pollution, and many garments are worn only a few times before being discarded. Moreover, workers in some supplier factories endure low wages and unsafe conditions. Consumers, the author argues, should consider buying fewer but better-made items.

Many Roman structures, including harbour walls built in seawater, have survived for around two thousand years, while modern concrete often begins to crack within decades. Researchers studying Roman concrete found that it contains volcanic ash and small lumps of lime. When cracks form and water seeps in, these lumps appear to react chemically and fill the gaps, allowing the material to repair itself. Engineers are now exploring whether similar principles could make modern concrete more durable.

Unstructured play, in which children invent their own games without adult direction, is declining in many countries as schedules fill up with organised activities and screen time. Child development experts consider this worrying. Through free play, children learn to negotiate rules, solve problems and manage risks, skills that are difficult to teach formally. Some experts even link the decline of free play to rising anxiety among young people, although this connection has not been proven.

Artificial light at night has transformed human life, but it also affects the natural world. Migrating birds, which navigate by the stars, can become disoriented by brightly lit buildings, and newly hatched sea turtles may crawl towards streetlights instead of the sea. In humans, exposure to bright light late in the evening can disrupt sleep. Unlike many environmental problems, however, light pollution is easy to reverse: shielding lamps and switching off unnecessary lights produces immediate results.

Roughly one third of all food produced in the world is lost or wasted. In poorer countries, most losses occur during storage and transport, owing to a lack of refrigeration and proper roads. In richer countries, by contrast, the largest share is thrown away by shops and households, often because of confusing date labels or overly strict standards for the appearance of fruit and vegetables. Reducing this waste would ease pressure on land and water resources.

The glaciers of the Himalayas are sometimes called Asia's water towers, because their meltwater feeds rivers on which more than a billion people depend. As temperatures rise, these glaciers are shrinking at an accelerating pace. In the short term, faster melting may actually increase river flows, but scientists warn that once the glaciers have significantly diminished, water supplies during dry seasons could decline sharply, with grave consequences for agriculture.

Electric vehicles are often promoted as the solution to transport emissions, and they do produce far less pollution over their lifetime than petrol cars. Yet their batteries depend on minerals such as lithium and cobalt, whose extraction can damage ecosystems and, in some places, involves poor working conditions. Recycling old batteries and developing new chemistries that use more abundant materials could reduce these problems, but neither solution is yet operating on a large scale.

For decades after its discovery on clay tablets in Crete, the ancient script known as Linear B defied all attempts at decipherment. Most scholars assumed it recorded an unknown language. In 1952, an English architect and amateur linguist, Michael Ventris, demonstrated that it was in fact an early form of Greek. His breakthrough pushed back the history of written Greek by several centuries and revealed that the tablets were mostly administrative records, such as lists of goods.

Caregivers have long observed that people with advanced dementia, who may no longer recognise their own relatives, can often sing songs from their youth word for word. Researchers suggest that musical memories may be stored in brain regions that are relatively spared by the disease. Programmes that play personalised music to patients have reported reduced agitation and improved mood. While music cannot halt the progress of dementia, it may significantly improve patients' quality of life.

Noise is often dismissed as a mere annoyance, but a growing body of research suggests that long-term exposure to loud traffic or aircraft noise can harm health. People living near busy roads or airports have higher rates of high blood pressure and sleep disturbance. Children in schools under flight paths have been found to learn to read more slowly. The World Health Organization now ranks noise as one of the most important environmental threats to health in Europe.

Not all scientific research is carried out by professionals. In citizen science projects, members of the public help collect or analyse data, from counting birds in their gardens to classifying galaxies in online images. Such projects allow scientists to gather information on a scale that would otherwise be impossible. Participants, meanwhile, gain a better understanding of science. Admittedly, data collected by amateurs may contain errors, but careful project design and multiple checks can minimise this problem.

Wolves were eliminated from Yellowstone National Park in the early twentieth century. In their absence, elk populations grew and overgrazed young trees along rivers. When wolves were reintroduced in 1995, elk numbers fell and the animals began avoiding certain areas. Some researchers argue that this allowed trees to recover, which in turn benefited birds and beavers. Others believe the effect has been exaggerated and that factors such as climate also played a role. The debate continues.

With laptops now common in lecture halls, many students take notes by typing. Some studies, however, suggest that students who write notes by hand remember the material better. Because handwriting is slower, it seems to force learners to summarise and rephrase information rather than copy it word for word, a process that deepens understanding. Typing is not necessarily inferior, researchers note, if students deliberately avoid transcribing lectures verbatim.

Tea arrived in Britain in the seventeenth century as an expensive luxury enjoyed mainly by the wealthy. Heavy taxes meant that much of the tea consumed was smuggled into the country. When the government sharply reduced the tax in 1784, smuggling became unprofitable almost overnight, and tea became affordable for ordinary people. By the nineteenth century, it had become a national habit, and the afternoon tea ritual had developed among the upper classes.

A growing number of countries have introduced taxes on sugary drinks in an effort to combat obesity. Evidence from places such as Mexico and the United Kingdom indicates that such taxes can lower consumption, and in some cases manufacturers have reformulated their products to contain less sugar. Opponents argue that the taxes fall disproportionately on poorer households and that obesity has many causes beyond soft drinks. Supporters respond that the revenue can be used to fund health programmes.

In 1977, scientists exploring the ocean floor near the Galápagos Islands made a startling discovery: communities of giant tubeworms, clams and crabs thriving around hot springs, known as hydrothermal vents, more than two kilometres below the surface. In total darkness, these ecosystems depend not on sunlight but on bacteria that obtain energy from chemicals in the vent water. The find overturned the belief that all life on Earth ultimately relies on the Sun.

Before the electric telegraph, news could travel no faster than a horse or a ship. When telegraph lines spread across continents in the mid-nineteenth century, messages that had taken weeks to deliver could be sent in minutes. Businesses used the technology to coordinate trade, governments to direct armies, and newspapers to report distant events on the same day. In many ways, the telegraph was the first step towards the connected world we live in today.

People who volunteer regularly tend to report higher life satisfaction and, according to some studies, may even live longer. Researchers suggest several reasons: volunteering provides a sense of purpose, strengthens social connections and encourages physical activity. However, the benefits appear to depend on motivation. In one study, people who volunteered mainly to help others enjoyed health benefits, whereas those who did so chiefly for their own advantage did not.

Hundreds of millions of people in rural Africa have no connection to an electricity grid. Extending power lines to remote villages is extremely costly. In recent years, however, small solar systems, often paid for in instalments via mobile phones, have brought electricity to millions of homes. Families can now charge phones, light their homes at night without kerosene lamps and, in some cases, run small businesses. Such systems cannot yet power heavy machinery, but they represent a significant improvement.

Between roughly 800 and 900 AD, many of the great cities of the Classic Maya in Central America were abandoned. The causes of this collapse have long puzzled researchers. Evidence from lake sediments points to a series of severe droughts during this period. Many scholars believe that drought, combined with overpopulation, deforestation and warfare between cities, overwhelmed Maya society. It is worth noting, however, that the Maya people did not disappear; millions of their descendants live in the region today.

The human gut contains trillions of bacteria, collectively known as the microbiome. Once regarded simply as passengers, these microbes are now known to help digest food, produce certain vitamins and train the immune system. Diet has a strong influence on their composition: a diet rich in fibre tends to support a more diverse microbial community. Scientists are investigating links between the microbiome and conditions ranging from obesity to depression, though many findings remain preliminary.

Japan experiences hundreds of earthquakes every year, and its building codes are among the strictest in the world. Many modern skyscrapers in Tokyo rest on base isolators, large rubber and steel bearings that allow the ground to move beneath a building while the structure itself sways gently. Others contain massive dampers that absorb vibrations. Thanks to such technologies, even very strong earthquakes have caused relatively little damage to recent buildings, although older structures remain vulnerable.

In 2016, Japanese scientists identified a bacterium that can break down PET, a plastic widely used in drinks bottles. Since then, researchers have modified the enzymes produced by such bacteria to work much faster. Some companies hope to use them to recycle plastic into new materials of the same quality, something conventional recycling struggles to achieve. Experts caution, though, that such technologies are no substitute for reducing plastic use in the first place.

Until the nineteenth century, most towns kept their own local time, based on the position of the sun. This caused little trouble when travel was slow, but the spread of railways made it a serious problem: timetables became confusing, and the risk of collisions increased. In 1884, an international conference in Washington established a system of standard time zones, with the prime meridian passing through Greenwich in London.

The Amazon rainforest recycles much of its own rainfall: trees release moisture into the air, which then falls again as rain further west. Some scientists warn that if deforestation and warming continue, parts of the forest could pass a 'tipping point', beyond which they would gradually turn into dry savanna. Such a change would release vast amounts of carbon and could be very difficult to reverse. Estimates of when this might occur vary widely, but many researchers argue that the risk justifies urgent action.

The earliest surviving photograph, taken in France around 1826, required an exposure time of several hours, which is why it shows only buildings and no people. Over the following decades, improvements in chemistry reduced exposure times to seconds, making portraits possible. By the end of the nineteenth century, cheap handheld cameras allowed ordinary people to take their own pictures, transforming photography from a specialist craft into a popular hobby.

After the Indian Ocean tsunami of 2004, which killed more than 200,000 people, countries around the region built a warning system based on seismic sensors and ocean buoys. The buoys detect changes in sea level and send data by satellite to warning centres. However, technology alone is not enough. Experts stress that people living on the coast must also know how to respond, for example by moving to higher ground immediately after feeling a strong earthquake, since the first waves can arrive within minutes.

The idea that 'laughter is the best medicine' has some scientific support. Laughing appears to reduce levels of stress hormones, relax muscles and temporarily increase tolerance of pain. It also strengthens social bonds, since people laugh far more often in company than alone. Nevertheless, researchers point out that many studies in this area are small, and that laughter should be regarded as a complement to medical treatment, not a replacement for it.

Ancient Egyptian doctors were famous throughout the ancient world. Medical papyri dating back more than 3,500 years describe the treatment of wounds, broken bones and eye diseases. Some remedies, such as applying honey to wounds, had genuine value, since honey has antibacterial properties. Others were based on magic and prayer. Egyptian medicine thus combined careful observation with religious beliefs, a mixture that was typical of the period.

The oceans absorb roughly a quarter of the carbon dioxide released by human activities. While this slows global warming, it comes at a cost: when carbon dioxide dissolves in seawater, it makes the water more acidic. This makes it harder for creatures such as corals, oysters and some plankton to build their shells and skeletons. Because many marine food chains depend on these organisms, scientists fear that acidification could have far-reaching effects on ocean life.

In 2003, London introduced a daily charge for driving into the city centre during working hours. In its first years, traffic in the zone fell by around a fifth, and bus services became faster and more reliable. The revenue was invested in public transport. Critics complained that the charge hurt small businesses and that congestion gradually returned as road space was reallocated to buses and cyclists. Nonetheless, several other cities have since adopted similar schemes.

Reading novels is usually seen as a leisure activity, but some psychologists believe it can also sharpen social skills. When readers follow the thoughts and feelings of fictional characters, they may be practising the ability to understand other people's perspectives. In several experiments, participants who read literary fiction performed slightly better on tests of empathy than those who read non-fiction. However, other researchers have failed to replicate these results, so the question remains open.

Pacific salmon hatch in freshwater streams, migrate to the ocean, and years later return to spawn in the very stream where they were born, sometimes travelling thousands of kilometres. Scientists believe they use the Earth's magnetic field to find the right stretch of coast, and then their sense of smell to identify their home river. Dams, however, can block these journeys, and some rivers have installed fish ladders to allow salmon to pass.

Many well-meaning people put items in recycling bins in the hope that they can be recycled, even when they are unsure. This practice, sometimes called 'wish-cycling', can actually do more harm than good. Greasy pizza boxes, plastic bags and broken glass can contaminate entire loads of recyclable material, which may then have to be sent to landfill. Checking local recycling rules, although less satisfying, is far more helpful.

Around one in five workers in industrialised countries works night shifts, including nurses, factory workers and pilots. Working at night forces the body to operate against its internal clock, which regulates sleep, hormone levels and digestion. Long-term night work has been associated with higher risks of obesity, heart disease and some cancers. Experts recommend measures such as limiting consecutive night shifts and keeping bedrooms completely dark during daytime sleep.

Hydrogen is often described as a clean fuel because using it produces only water. However, most hydrogen today is made from natural gas in a process that releases carbon dioxide. 'Green' hydrogen, produced by splitting water with renewable electricity, avoids these emissions but is currently much more expensive. Many experts believe hydrogen will be most useful in sectors that are hard to electrify, such as steelmaking and shipping, rather than in private cars.

Since the launch of the first satellite in 1957, thousands of objects have been left in orbit around the Earth, from dead satellites to tiny fragments of paint. Travelling at several kilometres per second, even a small piece of debris can seriously damage a working satellite or spacecraft. Scientists warn that collisions could create more fragments, triggering a chain reaction that might make some orbits unusable. Several companies are now testing ways to remove debris.

In the 1960s, the introduction of high-yield crop varieties, chemical fertilisers and irrigation dramatically increased food production in countries such as India and Mexico. This 'Green Revolution' is credited with preventing widespread famine. It also had drawbacks, however: heavy use of fertilisers and pesticides polluted soil and water, and irrigation depleted groundwater in some regions. Today, scientists are seeking ways to raise yields that are less damaging to the environment.

In 1997, the chess computer Deep Blue defeated the world champion Garry Kasparov, a moment widely seen as a milestone for artificial intelligence. Rather than killing interest in the game, computers have transformed it. Players of all levels now use chess programs to analyse their games and prepare for opponents, and online play has attracted millions of new players. Some even argue that human chess has become more creative, as players explore ideas suggested by machines.

Wildfires are usually seen as disasters, and near towns they certainly are. Yet in many ecosystems, fire is a natural and even necessary process. Some pine species produce cones that open and release their seeds only after being exposed to intense heat. Fires also clear dead vegetation and return nutrients to the soil. Paradoxically, decades of suppressing every small fire can allow fuel to build up, making later fires far more intense.

In the 1840s, the Hungarian doctor Ignaz Semmelweis noticed that women giving birth in a ward run by doctors died of fever far more often than those in a ward run by midwives. He realised that doctors often came directly from performing autopsies and suggested that they wash their hands with a chlorine solution. Death rates fell dramatically. Tragically, many of his colleagues rejected his ideas, and his work was fully appreciated only after his death.

Elephants communicate using a remarkable range of sounds, including low-frequency rumbles that are below the range of human hearing. These infrasonic calls can travel several kilometres, and researchers believe elephants may also detect them through their feet as vibrations in the ground. This ability allows separated family groups to coordinate their movements over long distances. Understanding such communication, conservationists argue, could help protect elephants from conflict with humans.

In recent years, minimalism, the idea of living with fewer possessions, has attracted a large following, particularly among young urban professionals. Supporters claim that owning less reduces stress, saves money and benefits the environment. Critics note, however, that minimalism is sometimes marketed as a lifestyle product in itself, complete with expensive 'minimalist' furniture, and that choosing to own little is a luxury unavailable to people who cannot afford basic necessities.
